utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. This is case number IT-97-25-T, the Prosecutor versus Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Krnojelac, we're in a different courtroom. Are you able to hear the proceedings in a language which you understand?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Please sit down. Now, there are a number of matters which the Prosecution have raised which we've got to deal with at this stage before the witness comes in. Just a moment while I find my papers. I think the Prosecution's application for videolink would be the first to deal with. Is that yours, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We filed this motion, and we have explained in the motion the details, why we want this motion to be raised -- this decision be made. However, there is one change. The Witness 115 does not testify at all. So that leaves us only with the Witness 49, and this witness is of special relevance, and, therefore, we still hold to our motion because this witness actually is a witness the accused himself refers to in his interview he had given to the Prosecutor's Office, and how this person got released, and why he was released and who was involved in it is of special relevance to the Prosecution case, and, therefore, we would like to keep this motion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In relation to 49 only.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, in relation to 49 only.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Does the Defence have any objection to that application?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, Your Honour, we have no objections. Of course, it would have been better to have the witness testify here, but if that is impossible, then we accept that he gives his testimony by videolink.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Is this the one that needs face distortion, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff? It's not, apparently. That caused a few technical problems, I understand. Very well. Then we'll make the orders sought by deleting from the draft the words "and FWS-115." If you need it in writing, it can be amended and presented for signature later on today. Now, that videolink is sought for a particular day, but it's not in the order. What date was it?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The day is the 30th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: 13th.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: 30th of January.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Very well. That's the first matter. Now, both parties have apparently spoken to the legal officers about the issue of what they call scheduling. I'm not sure that "scheduling" is the right word. There is a schedule that simply tells us what hours we're sitting. I don't think it's appropriate to have scheduling orders identifying precisely when there will be breaks. That's a matter that can be dealt with quite informally. Anybody who's had any experience in appearing in a criminal trial will realise that you cannot run a long trial day after day after day without having some time for preparation for future matters and to clean up messes that have been made in the past. So the Trial Chamber is very alive to your need. What we would prefer to do is to have it dealt with informally. If you speak to the legal officer, it can be dealt with between you, and if it can't be agreed, then we will have to determine it. We, of course, have other obligations to perform. Last year I remember it was very difficult to fit in a couple of Appeals Chamber matters into the one week that we had scheduled not to sit, and for that reason only, I would not agree to having that actually scheduled in advance. But the Trial Chamber does have some obligations in the week of the 5th of March. So that will be one week which we will suggest to you should be a break for both parties to be preparing matters for the future. How that fits in with the Prosecution's request for the week of the 19th of February, I'm not sure. If you had a break halfway in between that, it would be the week of the 5th of February, I think. Would you be able to make your investigations and go along to exert your persuasive influences upon these recalcitrant witnesses during the week of the 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. We need just one week, whenever it is. The 5th of March would be too late because we think we would already finish then with our Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. But how about the 5th of February?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The 5th of February would be fine.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: In case there's some problem, which you can raise with Mr. Roberts, it looks as though we will have those two weeks off for you to do work outside court. But anyway, you talk to Mr. Roberts and get it sorted out between you. Now, the next matter, Mr. Bakrac, if you remember, you reserved the situation in relation to the investigator's evidence, Mr. -- the Finnish gentleman, Mr. Kamppainen, I think his name was. You'll remember he introduced some further names which were not on Schedule C, and you said you wanted to use the Christmas break to investigate those. Have you finished those investigations?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, part of the team which is on the ground in Yugoslavia dealing with this, we did check one part of it and I believe we shall be able to round it off until the next break. I believe that the situation will be quite clear by that time. So we would prefer, we would beg you to allow us to give you our opinion at the end of this part of trial, that is, right before the next break. Besides, Your Honour, I'm not quite sure I understood it quite well, but it would be the week between the 5th of February and which other date that you envisage a break in this trial?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What I was suggesting was the week commencing the 5th of February, the whole of that week, and the week commencing the 5th of March, the whole of that week. So there will be four weeks now where we sit, a week off, three weeks, and then another week off. That's the proposal that I've put up, and I'm happy to hear anything that you want to say to Mr. Roberts about it. I just don't want to deal with it in court, that's all.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honour, that is what I discussed just before we started. I do think that the matter can be resolved with Mr. Roberts and I do not really wish to insist on that topic. I have nothing else to add. During the break, we shall talk to Mr. Roberts about this long break in the trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The point that I want to clear up or, if necessary, reserve is whether you want the investigator to be produced for further cross-examination, and there's the status of the document which was marked, from memory, 55/2. Those were the names which would otherwise have been part of Schedule C to the indictment but are being added by the Prosecution because they now have the names. They did not have them before.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. Perhaps there was some misunderstanding. I have asked, since we shall have a break and then the Prosecution's case will be resumed, then we would appreciate it if, by the end of that week in February, we can answer whether we shall need the investigator for the cross-examination, so that he could then come after the break.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Certainly that seems to be appropriate, but that would be, I think, the last possible opportunity you will have to investigate it, and after that it will go into evidence. Now, the Prosecution have indicated they want some protective measures for one of the witnesses coming up this week; 182, I think it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: This witness is a displaced person and lives in the former Yugoslavia, and he has requested a pseudonym and image alteration because he fears -- his status is quite unclear where he lives, and he fears that he has to return to Foca in the very near future. At the moment, a lot of displaced persons within Bosnia are pressured to go back to Foca, and he fears retaliation for himself, his family, especially his children.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I don't recall the precise details of that report that has been in evidence in another case, but I think I am right in saying that Foca was one of the areas where there has been a problem of people returning.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour. And we have explained also the reasons in our motion when we requested the protective measures for the other witnesses, and it's simply a similar case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: The same. Yes, thank you. What's the attitude of the Defence to that, Mr. Bakrac? This is Witness 182. They want a pseudonym and face distortion -- facial distortion.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, very briefly, we hold an identical view as with regard to other witnesses for whom protection was sought. Not to repeat it, we have the same objection as in earlier cases as regards the possibility of the Defence to check it all. But, of course, it is up to the Chamber to decide.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, I think you'll find that the result will be the same. But may I warn you that when you seek some protective measures for your witnesses, the Prosecution may come back with your argument. Very well. Those orders will be made in relation to Witness 182. Now, Mr. Bakrac, you have sought an order that the Trial Chamber have your client examined, and the Prosecution has taken the point, which, if I may say so, is a good one, that you have not identified to what issue such an examination would be relevant. Are you able to identify that issue for us now or would you like to put it in writing so that we can consider it later on in the week?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I can do so right now, but we have already written a brief, and I believe that the Chamber will receive it in the course of this day. In it, we gave our reasons in detail why we are asking for it. If you wish me, I shall explain it to you now verbally.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If we can deal with it today and we've got it in writing, don't worry. We won't waste time here. If there is any need for any argument upon it, then we can call upon you. Now, there's also some discussions between the parties about witnesses being called or the transcript of their evidence in the Kunarac trial being tendered. And I'm not sure, Mr. Bakrac, from your response whether you are objecting to the mere transcript going in or whether you are saying that provided you can cross-examine the witness, you do not mind the evidence that he gave or -- he or she gave in the Kunarac case being tendered as if it had been the evidence given in this trial. Which is it that you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, we accepted the Prosecution's proposal which concern three witnesses. We accepted the proposal regarding the FWS-33, that is, that the transcript of that witness's testimony in the Kunarac case be admitted as evidence in this case provided the Prosecution agrees that the testimony of a Defence witness from the same case, (redacted), be -- that is, that the transcript of his testimony be admitted as evidence without cross-examination because they both testified to the same -- about the same circumstances. The subject is the same. So we've decided that we can accept the transcript of Witness 33 if the transcript of the testimony of this other witness is also accepted, that is, Witness 33. As for the other two witnesses proposed by the Prosecution, we think we are of the opinion --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Can I just check with you? It's Witness DC you want to have as the quid pro quo. I'm sorry if that doesn't translate. You will accept 33, provided the Prosecution accept DC, without further cross-examination?

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Is that correct, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: 96 and what looks like 5 --

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, I apologise. Perhaps Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. the interpretation was wrong. We accept the FWS-33. We agree that the transcript be admitted without cross-examination, but we are also asking the Prosecution to accept the transcript of the Witness DC, again without cross-examination. That was a Defence witness in that same case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes. Well, now, there are two other witnesses that the Prosecution want to have their evidence tendered, the transcript of their evidence tendered, and that's 96 and 5. If you say you want them to be cross-examined, they will have to be produced for cross-examination. That's the usual course. But I think what we're trying to do is to save the time of them having to give their evidence again. So that the transcript of their evidence in Kunarac will be tendered, but they will be produced here for you to see them and cross-examine them.

utterances.speaker: MR. BAKRAC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, Your Honours. As regards these two other witnesses, we insisted that we cross-examine them, so to call them to come here. At a Pre-Trial Conference we agreed that these transcripts be admitted as evidence, but also with the possibility of cross-examining them. But we have decided that we do not need to cross-examine Witness 33. But as for these other two witnesses, we insist on their cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. Well, now, Ms. Uertz-Retzlaff, what about the quid pro quo? Are you happy to accept DC as a witness on the same basis?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, we do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, then, those two, the evidence can be entered at the appropriate stage. In relation to the other two, you want 96 and 5, it is accepted that provided that their evidence is tendered, their evidence from Kunarac is tendered, and they are produced for cross-examination. Are you happy with that?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Your Honour, in relation to the Witness 96, she -- I would -- we would rather prefer to have the witness not here, and I was wondering if I can make another suggestion. My understanding is that the reason why you want to cross-examine her is the part where she mentions Mr. Krnojelac. Is that the part that you want to cross-examine her on? I mean, we would also be willing to say we can strike this part of her testimony, because what we want to avoid is actually to have this very old lady, and she is also in a bad health condition, we would like to avoid to have her travelling here. And if that is an option for you, that we strike this portion of her testimony where she refers to the accused, we would be fine with that. And in relation to the Witness 05, this witness would have to be -- would have to testify through videolink. He's a very sick person. He has tuberculosis, and would we would have to go to the country where this person is living and would have to have a videolink conference. We tried to avoid it. That is why we also didn't want 33. And we would even be willing also to drop the other witness, the Witness 02, because this is also a candidate for videolink in that same country because of his ill-health, and we would be willing to drop this person knowing that videolink is a complicated and a time-consuming matter.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I was going to ask you that. This country where 05 is living, is there any problem with the videolink from there?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I do not think so, but we have three witnesses. These three witnesses, 33, 05, and 02, in this country, and they live in different parts of the country. So that would mean two videolinks now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: And the only reason actually why we would have -- we find 05 very important is that this person was very briefly in the KP Dom and he was released, and he got release papers showing who was making this decision. It's actually the release papers that are of the special relevance for the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are they signed?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, they are signed. Therefore, we actually asked to put in these papers without having the witness testify.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are they signed by Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, they are not signed by Mr. Krnojelac. They are signed by the Krizni Stab who made this decision.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Did 05 give evidence by videolink in Kunarac?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: But something has happened to his health since, is that what you're saying?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. The witness was not a witness in Kunarac. We have only a witness statement given to the Prosecutor's Office, and we say we can -- we can simply drop the witness. We don't need necessarily to produce his evidence, his verbal evidence, but we want to put in the documents he provided to the Prosecutor; that is, the document ID 65 and ID 66.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: What is the significance, if I may ask you, of the identity of the person who made the decision to release 05 from custody if it's not Mr. Krnojelac?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: But it shows the -- who was above the institution KP Dom, who was actually the superior of Mr. Krnojelac.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: I see. Right. Well, has there been some discussion with Mr. Bakrac on this basis? I, frankly, do not want to be trying to persuade one party or the other to accept something. If we have to make a ruling, we'll make a ruling. But it seems to me that if that's the only issue upon which you want to call the witness and if there can be no real dispute about the identity of the person who signed it, there is no need to call the witness, but that's a matter for some discussion between counsel, I think, before we have to rule on it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes, Your Honour, I think we will need -- we will use the break to discuss it further on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That's very good. Now, in relation to this correspondence that has passed between the parties, we are very grateful that the parties are actually talking to each other in this way. But if they want us to have a look at this correspondence in any way as argumentative material, it should be filed. In relation to the letter from Mr. Bakrac and Mr. Vasic of the 26th of December, there's a reference to the name of a witness who I think actually Mr. Bakrac did mention this morning too and it has had to be redacted from the transcript. Please, when you are talking to each other, use the pseudonyms so that if they do have to be filed, it's much easier rather than having to have them redacted even to file them. But, Mr. Bakrac, you did mention this name this morning, I gather, so do be careful. All right. Is there anything else we can dispose of before we continue with the witness that was partially heard?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: The Prosecution has requested a summons for one witness --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Oh, yes.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: -- for one particular witness, and we also left an alternative to this. We actually want this witness to testify in the Prosecution case and therefore we would need the summons. But on the other hand, the Defence, as we know from this witness, also wants to have this witness testify in their own case. That is at least the understanding of the witness. Now, we wonder --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does it matter?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: No. We only wondered if this is actually an opportunity to have a witness summoned as a Court witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that raises a number of very interesting problems. Has it ever been actually done?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: I think in other cases there were some Court witnesses, but they were heard after the parties had concluded their cases. Therefore, we rather would prefer it the other way around, that is, the witness testifies in the Prosecution case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: If you are talking about Blaskic, there were orders made which the witnesses were happy to comply with for the mere fact that they had been made. But looking at it, I see a number of problems which I think we're going to have to sort out. What is the difference between a subpoena and a witness summons? That's the first thing. You've asked for a witness summons. A subpoena is an order to a witness to give evidence under pain or penalty if he does not. If we issued a subpoena, and there's a bit of law discussing this, we would then have to be in a position to, in some way, punish him or her if the witness does not attend in accordance with the order, the subpoena. I'm not quite sure how we would do that. We can't send somebody in to arrest him like you do in domestic jurisdictions. What we would have to do, I suppose, is to make an application to the country where he is residing for them to arrest the witness and to produce the witness to us. If the country doesn't do it, we would have to report them or have the Tribunal report them to the United Nations, which I think by the time all that's done, the case will be over. A witness summons, if it is something different from a subpoena - I'm not quite sure what the difference is - it may be that there is no penalty if they do not turn up. I'm wondering whether that is something you really want here. Many witnesses, of course, have said they will turn up, provided that they can produce something to their employer to say they are required to attend. We have issued many orders along those lines but without any contemplation of having to enforce them if they do not comply with them. Now, have you investigated any of this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: We actually wanted to avoid the problems that the subpoena would cause, and therefore we requested a summons. What we hope is that when the summons is actually produced to the witness, that this witness then is willing to testify. That is actually also a reason why we wanted this break in February, to do that. We hope that the witness would then be willing to come.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, if you want to use it solely as some sort of legal justification for the witness to say, "Well, I'm now obliged to attend," I suppose we can do that. But I really am concerned should you seek to have it enforced in some way. When is it that you propose to call this witness? It's not until sometime in February, as I understand it.

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Yes. We wanted this witness to be summoned for the 26th of February.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: And both parties want him to be here, as I understand it. I'm not sure what the difference would be except one party will have the right to cross-examine and the other one will not, or may not. So it would probably be, from the accused's point of view, better for the Prosecution to call the witness, and if necessary, you may have some certain rights to cross-examine, but then the Defence can cross-examine him. Has there been any discussion between the parties in relation to this?

utterances.speaker: MS. UERTZ-RETZLAFF
utterances.text: Not yet, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, perhaps you might take the opportunity at one of the breaks during the hearing today or tomorrow to discuss this, and then if necessary, we can consider it so we know precisely the basis upon which you want it. That's what I'm concerned about. All right. Is there anything else? Well, we had part heard Witness 162. Witness 162 has protective measures so we'll need to pull the blinds down while the witness comes in. Ms. Kuo, you were taking the witness and you had finished, as I understood it; is that so?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: That's correct, Your Honour. The witness is just for cross-examination.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Now, sir, you are still bound by the solemn declaration which you took last year, the last century, the last millennium; do you understand that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, sit down, please, sir. Who's taking this witness? Mr. Vasic?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: I would like to wish the witness a good morning and introduce Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. myself. My name is Miroslav Vasic, I'm an attorney-at-law, and I'm one of the Defence counsel for the accused Milorad Krnojelac. Let us start with the cross-examination. In your statement, in response to the questions put by my learned colleague, you said that when the commodities were taken from the warehouse of your company, you said that you informed the director of the directorate about this. Could you tell us about the ethnicity of this person? What was he?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: We cannot hear the answers.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation]

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you tell me, in 1992, at that time, who was the commander of TO Foca, if you know, and what was his ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I think he was a Serb. I'm not sure but I think he was a Serb. I know that if the Chief of Police is a Muslim, then the other person would be a Serb. That was the procedure usually. I'm not sure but --

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could something please be done with the witness' microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Vasic, the interpreters did not hear the answer to your first question so we'll have to get that answer. If you heard it, if you could give us what he said. But there's also a problem with the microphone somehow. It may not be close enough to the witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour. I shall repeat the previous question.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Are you able to tell us what the answer to the first one was? He gave an answer. It was, what was the ethnicity of the person who had taken the commodities away?

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. The witness said that the director was a Muslim.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Can we get this microphone put up closer to the witness? You can proceed, Mr. Vasic.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the Public Security Service in Sarajevo, did you state that the commander of the TO was Sulejman Pilav?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're right.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: What ethnicity was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Muslim.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: It's been a long time. It's been eight or nine years. I've forgotten.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you very much.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: May I just say one more thing? There were two types of reserves, you see. There were municipal reserves and republican reserves and some federal reserves. Where there were TO warehouses, there were federal reserves. I think there was macaroni there, and these resources were depleted. It was a man called Milojica/Radojica who was in charge of these reserves. He was the only one who gave instructions to have these commodities, these reserves, issued, and he's the only person who could have issued such orders.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: There is a problem with the witness' microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: One moment. We still have a problem with the microphone. Is it you can't hear or is there some interference with it?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It is as if the witness' microphone were not on at all. It is as if we hear a different kind of sound from the courtroom without the microphone at all, as if it's being picked up by another microphone or something.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Well, that's something technical.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: The technician is coming to the interpreter's booth to have it checked. Also, we are having voice distortion at the moment.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That may mean another channel, I'm not sure. But I can hear the witness if I turn up the volume on the microphone.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Could the witness please say something? We have one of the technical persons in the booth now.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sir, would you just give us your name -- sorry, not your name. If you could repeat your pseudonym, 162, please, so that the technician can check your microphone.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Does that mean that you can now hear the witness? From the interpreters' booth, can you now hear the witness?

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: If the witness could say something, then we can --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Would you repeat it again, please, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: It has been fixed apparently.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you very much. You may proceed, Mr. Bakrac.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your statement, you said that after being detained in the KP Dom Foca, you gave a statement to the investigations commission or, rather, the investigators from the investigations commission. What are you referring to, to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. It lasted for about 15 minutes. Not longer than that.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You talked about the investigations commission. Was this a military investigations commission?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. The president was there and I also said who the president was, Vladicic and there were two other members.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: And the statement that you gave in 1997 to the investigator of the OTP, did you say that Vladicic, Starovic, and Koprivica were members of the military investigations commission for detained persons?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know. They did not wear military uniforms at any rate, but possibly they were because later, when I was told or, rather, when he asked me why I went down there and all that, about 10 or 15 minutes I was with them, and I said why I went there. Then he took this piece of paper out of the typewriter and threw it into the wastepaper basket as if he said to me it was the military command that was supposed to talk to me. It was to that effect.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you. Did you state to the public security services in Sarajevo that Colonel Kovac personally came to take out the detainees named Cengic and that he took them out of the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. He was in the warden's office, this man Kovac, when the two Cengics went out for an interview. And he introduced himself by the name of Kovac. He said, "I'm Kovac."

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: This Colonel Kovac, did he take these persons away?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It was late. It was late on that day. I think it was the 15th of January. It was quite cold. And he said, "It's late this time, but tomorrow a car will come to pick you up at 8.00, I think." And exactly the next day at 8.00, Milutinovic, a guard, came and took them away.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Who said that? Who said that, that a car would come to pick them up the next day? The warden?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No, not the warden. Kovac did.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: He said that he personally got orders from Milosevic to take them to Belgrade.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Did you say to the investigators of the OTP, in the statement that you made, that conditions of accommodation, rather, that accommodation in the KP Dom was acceptable in view of the situation that then prevailed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Exactly.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In the statement that you gave to the public security station, did you state that together with you in Room 20 there were some eminent citizens of Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Was Mr. Safet Avdic in that room also?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. For a certain amount of time, yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Actually, in the later period, Safet was with us in that room. This was this one room where we were singled out. There were 12 to 15 persons in that room, and we were never reported to the Red Cross.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said here that you were physically abused, and in response to my learned colleague's question, you said that you did not state that to the public security station or the investigators of the Prosecution; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: If I remember correctly, I said, either in Sarajevo or I don't know where, that I was mistreated once. However, I did not consider that to be evil because I fared quite well compared to my colleagues. I thought that everything was fine. I was alive.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: When you made your statement to the public security station, were the members of your family present?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, they were not.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Can you explain to me then, how did you think that your children would find out about this event if you state this to the public security centre? Because in response to my learned colleague's question in terms of why you didn't state this earlier, you said that you were afraid that your children would find out.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I said that. I had a family, and I had my brothers and sisters in Gorazde, and my daughter was in Sarajevo. I was afraid. Gorazde was under siege. Sarajevo was under siege. It was shelled every day. And also when I was being exchanged, they told us in one sentence, "Be careful what you're saying because you may come back here." That was one of the motives.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Yes, sir, but that is a statement that you gave to the police of the Federation. What do you mean? How can this be interpreted to your children? The Defence believes that this is not very logical, especially to have this statement interpreted to the Serb side.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. It seems to me that I said in one sentence that I was mistreated once, and I think that took care of that. Also, in Sarajevo, when I gave my statement, there were shells that were falling, and I didn't know where I was. I was still obsessed. I still thought that I was in the camp. Shells were falling. The siege of Sarajevo was still on. I wanted to give this statement as soon as possible, and I wanted to leave because I was sick.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Witness, even if that were so in 1994, why didn't you say that in 1997 to the investigator of the OTP when you knew that you would come to testify before this Tribunal, when you said so?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You know why? In 1997, I was in Sarajevo. I was visited by friends from Foca to came to visit me, and they said that they knew everything, everything that happened to me, that this man who beat me, who was not in the KP Dom at all and all of that. After that, when they said to me that they knew about it, I sort of thought, well, why shouldn't I talk about it too then? That was the only reason, nothing else.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Why didn't you say this to the investigators when you decided to speak up?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: That was after the investigators.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: It was after the investigators. And before that you thought that you would keep silent about that part?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, I didn't think that I would keep silent. I don't know. I -- I didn't want my children to know about it. I didn't want them to be traumatised and things like that. I mean, the suffering I experienced in the KP Dom is something that I did not want to transfer to my children.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Nevertheless, you decided to talk about this in front of the Tribunal here.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes. Yes. Well, if these people in Foca know, so why wouldn't these people know too.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Is it for the same reason that you spoke up only here in your testimony for the first time about details related to throwing bread away, taking bread out of the containers? You did not say this at the public security station or to the investigator of the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Well, this was discussed in detail here, what the food was like, et cetera. I said that I would be the happiest man alive if I would have a kilo of bread in my hands. That's the way it was. We ate whatever we could. We did not put any questions as to where the bread came from and all that. We just needed a bit more bread. Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: In your previous statements you also talked about food, but this detail about Serb prisoners throwing food, throwing bread out of the windows was not mentioned. Is that for the same reason why you did not say you were physically abused before?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. I just forgot that detail. I didn't think it was that important.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: You're welcome.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You said that you know that Munib Veiz, a prisoner, was taken out and was never returned. Can you tell us from which room he was taken out, when, and how come you know about this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know which room he was taken from. This was a different building, the one where he was, but prisoners told me about this. And his father was with me in the same room, Veiz's father.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Do you know when he was taken out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: On which day?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: I don't know.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: You don't know any closer details about this?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No, I don't.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. VASIC
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Your Honours, the Defence has no further questions for this witness in cross-examination. Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you. Any re-examination, Ms. Kuo?

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Just very briefly, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Witness, you were asked about Mr. Sulejman Pilav being the commander of the TO. Do you remember, do you know if he remained the commander of the TO once the war started?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: No. No. Everyone got away. No. Some kind of Crisis Staff was established then and there were other people there, in Ustikolina. They had actually withdrawn to Ustikolina, 12 kilometres away from Foca. That's where it is.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: Did you see Mr. Pilav in Ustikolina then?

utterances.speaker: FWS-162 [Resumed]
utterances.text: Yes, I did.

utterances.speaker: MS. KUO
utterances.text: No further questions, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Thank you, sir, for giving evidence. You may leave. Just wait for the blinds to be pulled down on that side of the room for you to leave the courtroom.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Mr. Smith, you have the next witness, do you? Is it a protected measures matter?

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Your Honour. Yes, I do have the next witness and protection measures have been granted, a pseudonym and image distortion.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Please take the solemn declaration, sir.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Sit down, please, sir. Usher, we'll need the microphones changed again.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Good morning, Witness. I know you're very anxious about giving your testimony this morning and I know you have a heart condition. So if you would like a break, if you could just ask the Judges for a break if you require it.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: There is a paper in front of you and it contains a number, the number 86, and it also contains your name below it and your date of birth. Are those details correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, you've been granted protective measures of your name so we'll only refer to your name as "86," and also the protective measure of image distortion; do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Also, there were two other names on that piece of paper with corresponding numbers on it. If you refer to those names in your testimony, could you refer to their number and not their name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: [In English] Okay.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Your Honour, I ask that that piece of paper be tendered as -- I think it's 405, Prosecution Exhibit 405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: That will be Exhibit 405.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: For the Court's information, this witness appears in Schedule D, at number 22 of the Schedule attached to the indictment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, what is your ethnic background?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I am a Muslim, a Bosniak by ethnicity.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When did the conflict in Foca occur in 1992? What date?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: In my assessment, there were certain overtures, but as far as I can remember, the actual shooting started on the 7th/8th of April, 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was the shooting between?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Surely there is no dispute about any of this, Mr. Smith. If you want him to go to a particular part, then lead him to it.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour. We'll move a bit faster then.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At the time that the conflict occurred, you lived in the town of Foca; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And you lived in the suburb of Deova Mahala.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: My parents lived in Mahala and I lived in a residential block in the very heart of the town. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You were living with your wife at the time, and your children were away, living outside of Foca.

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At that time, you held a (redacted) position at the Maglic company; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: It is, yes. (redacted)

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the main political parties in Foca at that time were the SDS and the SDA; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: In addition to those two chief parties, there were other parties. The reform party. But these two were the leading parties, the SDS and the SDA. There was also SDP, which was the reformist party, but its importance was symbolic compared with those two others.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who were the main political leaders of the SDS party at a local level in Foca?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: The chief political figures in the SDS at the time were Stanimir Stanic -- no, Stanic -- yes, Stanic. Miro, that's what they called him. He was the President of the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And he lived in Foca at that time?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: He did, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who was Petko Cancar?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Petko Cancar, as far as I can remember after all this time, was a member of the SDS, a member of its Main Board. But he also had a reputation of an important political figure in republican authorities, with their headquarters in Sarajevo, and enjoyed major prestige among those elected to the Assembly of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He truly enjoyed very high prestige in the SDS in the town of Foca or, rather, the municipality of Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Velibor Ostojic?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Velibor Ostojic was the Minister for Information in the government, in the Assembly, that is, the government of the Republic of Bosnia-Herzegovina. He was born some 30 kilometres away from Foca and had a particular weight in the SDS. I considered him one of the most responsible people for what happened in Foca.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Prior to the conflict, did he live in Sarajevo?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes, quite. Prior to the conflict, he frequently came to Foca but he resided in Sarajevo.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And Vojislav Maksimovic, who was he?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Vojislav Maksimovic was a high-ranking political figure. He was the President of the SDS club in the parliament of Bosnia-Herzegovina, and also enjoyed high prestige and pulled a great deal of weight and played a major role during the events which preceded the conflicts and then during the conflicts themselves.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: He lived in Sarajevo prior to the conflict; is that right?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes, yes, he lived in Sarajevo, but he came to Foca quite often because he also had a brother who lived near Foca, who worked there. His father's name was Jovo, and he had quite a number of friends on all sides, especially among Muslims. If you need it also, he was nominated for the parliament and a large number of Muslims had voted for him. But, of course, it turned out subsequently that they had made a major mistake, all those Muslim voters.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: In 1992, did either Mr. Maksimovic or Mr. Ostojic make any speeches, public speeches, in relation to the conflict that subsequently followed?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Everywhere, as far as I was informed, various promotional activities were taking place everywhere; that is, they were bringing together, rallying, their own peoples. One of those activities was at the stadium in Foca. When the SDS was established, there was this assembly and I attended it as a citizen. One wants to know certain things so as not to be misled, so on and so forth. I remember it very well to this day. There was Karadzic, Plavsic, Ostojic, Kilibarda, Maksimovic, Stanic, and others who came along with them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What night was this rally at the stadium, or what year?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Well, that was in 1991, and quite a number of things began to change as of then. Certain things changed very quickly. Many normal people couldn't really understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What was the main idea put forward by the SDS representatives at this rally in 1991? What was the main platform?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: The platform, from what I remember, it mostly had to do with the historical context, and its main purpose was a chauvinistic, a nationalistic incitement so as to create a nucleus, to create a core in the very being of the Serb people who did not want to be under the rule of Turks, because history knew that it was their turf, that it was their heritage and that they would not tolerate what they tolerated during the Turkish rule. That was the basis. They identified the Turkish rule with their neighbours who were of a completely different ethnicity but with whom they, nevertheless, lived as good neighbours, good friends, good fellow workers. And that was very, very hard to understand.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If we could move to March and April of 1992. Did any of these SDS politicians which you've mentioned make any nationalistic statements in 1992, around March or April?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Maksimovic, Ostojic, and others used to come very frequently, and other politicians from the SDS came too. Fortunately or unfortunately, (redacted), above the offices, where some of these activities were taking place, that is, meetings. And everybody, the SDA, SDS, reformists -- so that I had the opportunity -- so that I could see very many people go into those offices. I had a feeling that something happened every day with information which reached us through the local Foca radio station, and it was then transmitted to municipal authorities. The SDS had certain requests, that is, to split Foca into the Serb and Muslim part. Those were the demands. But then sometime in early April, there were daily meetings. They voted to finding/devising a peaceful solution. According to some who attended them, Zijo Ajanovic and others, who were members of the local board, the municipal government, from one minute to the other, these demands changed and they felt that it was all orchestrated by Ostojic. But they pursued such policy requesting complete disarmament of all Muslim individuals if they had any weapons.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. And what was the SDA leadership's response to these Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. intentions of the SDS leadership to split Foca into two?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Normal people simply could not conceive that, to build a new Berlin wall where there is no possibility for that. That was an imbecile thing for normal people. But the policy they wanted to put through resulted in some incidents, armed incidents. And as far as I can remember, the right-hand side, the whole right bank of the Drina was covered by paramilitary forces, heavy weaponry, and semi-heavy weaponry, and it began sometime around the 7th or 8th or 9th. Those were the three days which, as I remember, were crucial, when fire was opened on citizens in the town.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know which ethnic group these paramilitaries belonged to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: SDS had the possibility, and I remember it personally, they brought in semi-heavy artillery, and they transported those weaponry through the town in the late hours of the night, and they deployed that weaponry around the town. The SDS had all the weaponry of the Territorial Defence and all the other materiel and all or, rather, almost all of them were dressed in olive-grey JNA uniforms. Now, was that lawful or semi-lawful or paramilitary? But I, nevertheless, believed that it was their lawful army as proven by the fact that they lined up such men in front of the Ribarski, and that both Maskimovic and Ostojic, among others, were those who saluted them. Those who would not respond, and I saw that with my own eyes, those who would not respond, that is, those from Serb families who had failed to respond, who would fail to put on their uniform, and many had escaped to various places, to villages and other places, they were subsequently subjected to special treatment.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: If I can stop you there. Just prior to the conflict, was there any part of the population that seemed to arm themselves prior to the conflict in April 1992, in the months preceding? Was there a significant increase in arms in the Foca municipality?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Well, it would take some time to explain it properly. All I can say is that in 1992, in late 1992 and especially 1993 and the beginning of 1993 -- no. Excuse me. In 1991, that is, early 1992, owing to an incident which was a kind of an introduction to the solution of financial problems of the SDS, and they tried to resolve their financial problems by an incident called Focatrans, which was a trucking company. They formed their monoethnic company, and later, owing to their connections in the Maglic company and other companies, by so-called compensations in sawn timber, in exchange for that they brought from Serbia weapons and ammunition. There is information from stories that I heard that weapons, light weapons, were distributed on a large scale among the Serb population. Those weapons -- people took those weapons home. And the signal was to light a candle, which would be placed on the window. And an incident happened when by accident a Muslim man lit a candle and a Serb brought him a rifle by mistake. I remember well that story and the man when that happened. That was in January or perhaps February 1992.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Were the Muslim inhabitants of the Foca town or the Foca municipality arming themselves at the same rate as what the Bosnian Serbs were doing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: According to information, some Muslims were also armed, but not as fast and as much as in the case of the SDS. According to some information, I personally did not see that but I heard from quite a number of people, that they, that is Muslims, who wanted to have a rifle could pay 1.000 or 2.000 marks and buy a rifle from some people who had reportedly organised a paramilitary force in the SDA. And they were really comic situations; that is, there were some guys of Serb ethnicity who sold rifles for 50 marks, that is, as among pals or when they were short of money. That is what I also heard from different sources, and I should say that there was quite a lot of truth in that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you Witness. You stated that you believe the conflict occurred on the 7th of April, 1992. How did it start and where were you when it started?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Well, the -- it was on the 7th or perhaps the 8th, but I know it was Monday. My office was quite close to where I lived, and when I got there there was a policeman at the door. I asked the man, whom I knew, "What's up?" He said, "The radio station was taken last night. Last night some changes took place in the post office. Nobody can go there. And these key facilities have already been put under the control of the SDS."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Stop there for a moment. Did you see any violence on that day, on the 7th of April, any destruction or killing?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: No. Nothing happened that day of that particular nature, but later on I was able to go and buy newspapers, and one could see that there had been some shooting that day or that night in front of the -- in front of the army club or the army centre. There were some fired casings, which means that that night, between the 7th and the 8th, there already had been some armed incidents.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: After the conflict commenced in Foca, you were arrested some time later and taken to KP Dom; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what date was that?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: [Microphone not activated] ... remember. It's not easy for me to think about that. The 19th of April, 1.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And where were you when you were arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: With my wife and at times also with my neighbours. I was in the flat all the time, and I told you where that flat was. So until then, until about the 15th or 16th of April, I was in the flat. And I could not stand it any longer because there would be three or four strong groups - and I can't remember really - which would come to that flat - I don't know how many times - from early morning to the night, and then physically ill-treating us. They tried to slaughter me with a knife. They took me from one door to the other to show them who lived where, and in that way -- and they also had an automatic rifle and would fire at the door or, rather, at a lock so as to open the door, and to have me enter the flat first and see the situation there, whether there was any danger or not so that they could go in and take whatever they were interested in. And I went like that from one door to the other several times with an automatic pointed at me. And we could not stand any -- stand it any longer, and I then asked by telephone, because it worked, I called Jovo Milosevic to take us into their doorway because there were more Serb families there and they could perhaps have more influence and see that nothing happens to us. On the 15th or 16th, perhaps, after all my imprecations and after I implored him, he allowed us to move into the doorway. Then we moved into Dr. Zijo Ajanovic's flat, and we were sheltered there to a point. Then the 19th -- that is, we were also ill-treated there but much less. Later on, on the critical day, on the 19th, a group came and they took out all of us who were of Muslim ethnicity and took us to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Who was in that particular group that took you to the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: In that group were two brothers, (redacted). In the same car a man called Cosa drove us. I don't remember. I don't think I -- I don't think I ever saw him before, but I just heard that they were calling him Cosa. Me and Nezir Coric. And that day he only told us that he was taking us so that we could give statements, and he would bring us back. At their urging and trusting them, I left in another man's slippers and another man's sweater. It was cold. It was April, but it was very cold and it was as if it was the middle of winter.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Who was with Cosa? Who else was with Cosa that arrested you and took you to KP Dom? How many people arrived at the flat?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Four. They were from Foca and there were also others from -- what's it called? Uzice, Uzice Battalion that played the main role in all that.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Uzice is in Serbia?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you able to identify anyone else from that group, apart from Cosa, by name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: That day I saw two other armed men who were kind of helping, and it was Veljo, son of Vukadin. And I remember whether he used to work for the plywood and veneer factory, but I'm not quite sure. And there was another one, a yellow one. He looked yellow. And he was armed, and he was an electrician. I mean, I didn't know quite a number of those people because I moved in a completely different circle. And this influx, that is, SDS involved quite a number of outsiders, all those who were registered with all sorts of courts, the biggest criminals.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Witness.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: I think that is an appropriate time to break, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: When you see that the witness is going to refer to someone on your list, you better draw his attention to it because he has mentioned one of them already. The name has been redacted. We will adjourn now until 11.30.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: Yes, Mr. Smith.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honours.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Witness, just before we start, I know it's an anxious moment for you giving evidence in the court, but I would just ask if you could confine your answers to the specific question that I ask and then I will follow up with other questions, just so that we can get the most important points out as testimony to the Court. Do you understand?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You mentioned earlier that when you were in your apartment on about the 15th or 16th of April, 1992, there were some strong groups that came to your apartment, and on one occasion you were threatened with a knife. Where did those strong groups come from? What army?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Those groups came -- I mean, they were paramilitary forces, the White Eagles. They introduced themselves as such. And also there were Arkan's men. They were also accompanied by one of the members of the SDS from the town of Foca itself.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Arkan's men and the White Eagles, do you know which ethnicity they were? Were they Bosnian Muslim or Bosnian Serb or Serb or some other ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: They introduced themselves as such. Judging by their accent, I saw that they came from Serbia. Later on on several occasions, they even said themselves that they lived somewhere around Titovo Uzice.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When they came to your flat, what did they do? What was the purpose of their visit?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: The purpose of their visit was, first of all, to search us to see whether we, as the Muslim population, had any weapons. They searched our apartments thoroughly to see whether we had any weapons. In my case, there weren't any.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the last occasion, on the 19th of April, you were taken to the KP Dom. When you arrived at the KP Dom, what did you see outside of the facility? Were there any other soldiers, any other men there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes, yes, there were. Outside the building and in the part of that street that leads to KP Dom, I saw quite a few destroyed and burned buildings. But I also saw quite a few men in uniform who were in that area around the KP Dom, where there was a lot of outside security.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Now, the destroyed or burned buildings, do you know which ethnic group they belonged to, the owners? Bosnian Serb, Bosnian Muslim, or some other?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: This is the main street, the main artery that leads to the KP Dom. What I saw were, for the most part -- no, not for the most part, all of them, I mean these were mainly Muslim houses that were burned. But there were also other buildings that were burned that belonged to -- well, there were restaurants, like the Cafe Bor and other buildings that were used as restaurants. There were also some shop windows that belonged to Muslims. Some of the shop windows were broken and they belonged to shops belonging to Muslims.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: When you arrived at the KP Dom, the men that you saw in uniform, do you know which group they came from, which army or which ethnicity they belonged to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Well, on that critical day, when I came and when they threw us out in front of the door of the KP Dom, then one of the men had rank insignia of a Yugoslav army officer, but according to his accent, he was a member Blank page inserted to ensure pagination corresponds between the French and English transcripts. of the Montenegrin people. He hit me and said, "If they are fundamentalists, kill them immediately; if they are not, let them go home."

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How did he hit you? What did he hit you with?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: He hit me but he hit me with something, I mean so hard that I didn't have time to see. But my right arm and shoulder blade were black. It was hit so hard I couldn't even use my right hand to eat.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: The soldiers, did they come from Foca, the ones that were outside of the KP Dom, or did they come from another area?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: According to certain information, this was the Uzice Battalion, the active and reserve force. As they returned from Herzegovina, they had the task to take, together with the SDS, certain localities that were from the direction of Herzegovina to the direction of Foca, Gorazde, Rudo, Visegrad, Cajnice, Rogatica, et cetera.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were there any local residents outside with these Serbian soldiers that seemed to be working with them?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes. They were the ones in charge, I mean in charge of pointing things and people out, having them taken away. At first they were helped by these paramilitaries or, rather, reservists of the Yugoslav army.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: About how many soldiers were present outside the KP Dom when you arrived?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Well, they were deployed in this part of the street from the bakery onwards, and the bakery is about 150 to 200 metres away from the main entrance. I can't remember now. There were groups of 15, 20, 30, whatever. I wasn't really interested. They drove us pretty fast so that we would get to where we were going. But there were some groups of soldiers that were controlling the entrance to the KP Dom.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: You were taken inside the KP Dom. Were you registered? Were your details taken by anyone inside the KP Dom when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: I entered together with those three neighbours of mine, and at the main gate or, rather, the entranceway, on the left-hand side there was a reception. At the reception was a man who had this main logbook where he registered persons by their name, surname, father's name, address, place of birth. After that -- I mean, there was an escort all the time of two or three armed soldiers. They escorted us through the halls to the other building.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And the person that was taking the details in the registration book, was he a local from Foca or did you not know him?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what was his name?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes. His nickname was Cakani. But people know, everybody in Foca knows, but they used his nickname Cakani more than his name and surname. Everybody in Foca knew who that was.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did he work at the KP Dom before the conflict broke out?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes. Yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: As you were arrested and taken into KP Dom, did either this man Cakani or anyone else advise you why you were being detained there?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: No. No. He was not in charge of that. He was just in charge of the entrance. We were treated like commodities and it was as if commodities as entered.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you remember which room you were taken to on the first day that you arrived at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes. Yes, I remember very well. From that gate, or, rather from that reception when they took us through the halls to another gate, a metal gate, an iron gate that goes into the yard where the other buildings of the KP Dom are, then at the other gate we were registered once again by a man who belonged to the reservists of the Uzice Battalion. They called him Pisar, and he registered us again and he took all our personal belongings, our lighters, cigarettes, everything that belonged to us. Then he said, "If there are fundamentalists here they should be taken to number 12, to the quarantine, and if not to the left. The left, that is where they belong then." That was number 11 in that case.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And what room were you taken to?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: They just put us into an area in front of the toilet. Later, as we were waiting for statements to be taken - that's what they said - we saw an hour or an hour and a half later, after having waited for an hour, an hour and a half, we saw that nothing was actually going on. And accidentally a door opened and one man got out and wanted to go to the toilet, and he saw us, and he said, "What are you doing there? Why don't you go inside?" and then we went inside. And lo and behold, it turned out that in those rooms, according to some counts, there were about 170 persons. Ninety per cent of them were Muslims. There were three or four Catholics too.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you. Which room did you sleep in on the night of the 19th of April? Do you know the number of it?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: That was an area that consisted of four rooms or, rather, a fifth one too that was used while -- before the war, this was a normal prison. That room was used as a sitting room for watching television as well, which was quite normal. Those four rooms were different in size, and they also had different kinds of equipment or, rather, places where you could lie on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE HUNT
utterances.text: You were being asked what number the room was, if you know it. That was what the question was. Do you remember what number it was?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Eleven.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Thank you, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: On the inside of the KP Dom when you first arrived, who appeared to be in control of the detainees? Were they locals from Foca or are these army members, these soldiers from Uzice which you said you saw out the front or someone else? Which group appeared to be in control?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Well, at first I had the impression that all of this was organised by those reservists of the Uzice Battalion and that they were the ones who were in charge.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: At sometime later -- sorry, I withdraw that. At that time when you first arrived, did you see any local people from Foca, local civilian guards inside the KP Dom or not when you first arrived?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: On that day when I arrived, I saw some men who were wearing military uniforms, civilians, and these were the beginnings of -- I mean, I think, of the guard service. That's when they were initially organised. However, my feeling was that there was quite a bit of anarchy then and that the sole persons in charge were the reservists from the Uzice Battalion and the SDS provided certain services to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And did the soldiers from the Uzice Battalion leave at any stage? Did they leave KP Dom at some date later?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: I cannot recall the exact date, but I think that this went on possibly for 7 days or possibly 15 days. Ten or 15 days approximately that all this went on, until a service was established which then continued to function as such.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And when you say a service was established, who was in control of the detainees once this service was established? Were they locals from Foca? Were they people that worked at the KP Dom before or were they someone else?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: For the most part these were people who previously worked in certain services of the KP Dom, that is to say, before the conflict broke out or, rather, they were assisted by certain solutions provided by the SDS, that were imposed by the SDS.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Were you interviewed at any stage whilst you were at the KP Dom?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes. I remember that as if it were today. It was the 20th of April, 1992, sometime around 11.00.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And who interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: I was escorted by a guard. My name was called out by a guard. I was taken to the administrative building where there were persons who were in charge of interviews, the so-called investigators or investigation inspectors who had also worked as inspectors in the SUP or at that time already the MUP.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Do you know the names of the people that interviewed you?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: I do. Let me say straight away that this was a man I knew from the same company. He was a technician in the timber processing industry. He worked in Iverica for some time. His name was Petko Gasevic. And Zoran Vladicic actually interviewed me.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: What did they ask you basically?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: As far as I can remember, the statement contained several details of mine rather than what the main subject of the interview was supposed to be. The subject was whether I had any weapons at home, whether I purchased any weapons, if I purchased any weapons, who had I purchased them from, do I know who was selling weapons, et cetera. That was it. My answers were negative.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And then that was the truth; is that correct? You had no weapons and --

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: Yes, yes.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: -- you weren't a member of any military force or military group prior to being arrested?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: Did they tell you why you were being detained?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: No.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: How long did this interview last for?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: That interview lasted for either 30 or 40 minutes. It was not longer than that, at any rate.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
utterances.text: And that was recorded on a typewriter; is that correct?

utterances.speaker: FWS-86
utterances.text: No. It was typed on a typewriter that used the Cyrillic alphabet. Since I had to sign it, I saw that it was in Cyrillic. As far as I can remember, it said in the heading, "The Serb Republic," et cetera. That was the heading. All of it was according to the ideas of some of their leaders about the establishment of their state.

utterances.speaker: MR. SMITH
